author: Travis
title: KBS Is Betting Faster Swing Speeds Want Less Launch, Not Just More Weight
body:
Low-bend point construction in a 90-gram shaft is not a neutral engineering choice. KBS Golf Shafts introduced the Tour 90 this week, slotting it above the existing Tour 80 in weight and below the shaft's launch window, targeting faster-swing-speed players who want a penetrating ball flight without climbing into heavier profiles they don't need.

The core tension here is worth naming plainly. Conventional shaft wisdom has long held that faster swings get heavier steel, partly because heavier profiles resist twisting under load and partly because the added weight suppresses the ballooning flight that higher club head speed can produce. KBS is making a different argument: that the weight ceiling a player actually wants is dictated by feel and tempo, and that launch angle is a separate variable the shaft's bend point can control independently. That is a real engineering claim, not a marketing one, and it is largely defensible. The Dynamic Gold X100, at 130 grams, remains the benchmark for the heaviest-swing category precisely because its high bend point and stiff tip section suppress launch for elite ball strikers. KBS is offering a lighter entry to that same flight profile. Whether the bend point alone closes the gap is the question the fitting data will eventually answer.

Kim Braly founded KBS in 2005 after a long tenure at True Temper, and the KBS Tour franchise has spent the better part of fifteen years chipping away at Dynamic Gold's grip on the steel iron shaft market. That story is one of the more underreported share shifts in equipment. The Tour 80 gave KBS a foothold with players who wanted the control of a steel shaft without the weight penalty. The Tour 90, in three weight profiles from 90 to 100 grams across Stiff and X-Stiff only, extends that logic one step further: same flight philosophy, wider weight window, narrower flex range. The channel strategy, certified KBS fitting facilities and premium independents at $34.95 per shaft, keeps the product in environments where someone can actually match it to a swing rather than pull it off a rack.

The DORMIED Index has KBS up 18 percent month-over-month entering April, which tracks against a pre-launch cycle that tends to move shaft brands before retail availability hits. KBS also reported 14 tour winners on staff this season across all four major tours. Tour staff numbers are almost always a lagging marketing signal, but in the shaft category they matter more than in most, because a fitter leaning on tour validation to justify a recommendation is a real part of the purchase chain. The Tour 90 gives KBS something to point at for the specific conversation about launch angle that club fitters have with better players roughly every fitting session.

The sharper question for KBS is not whether the Tour 90 works but whether there are enough golfers in the swing-speed range who (a) want lighter steel, (b) want lower launch, and (c) can feel the difference well enough to seek it out. That is a narrower Venn diagram than the marketing language implies. Shaft companies that expand lines without expanding fitting access tend to add SKUs without adding revenue. KBS is protecting against that with its fitting-first retail strategy. If the certification network holds and fitters trust the positioning, the Tour 90 earns its place in the lineup. If it becomes shelf inventory at a premium retailer next to a True Temper Dynamic Gold that a fitter already knows how to sell, this launch is infrastructure the brand built for a customer it hasn't fully acquired yet.
